articles.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
articles.summary: Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.
articles.content:
Scientists at the University of Virginia Comprehensive Cancer Center have developed a promising experimental strategy for treating glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive malignant brain tumor in adults. The new approach could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles that have limited the effectiveness of existing brain cancer treatments.

The research team, led by UVA's Roger Abounader, MD, PhD, identified tiny genetic molecules known as "microRNAs" that can interfere with several genes responsible for the development and growth of glioblastoma. To deliver these molecules into the brain, the researchers combined specialized nanoparticles, focused ultrasound and microscopic bubbles. Together, these technologies offer a way to temporarily cross the brain's protective barrier, which normally prevents many treatments from reaching brain tumors and other neurological conditions.

"This new approach could help target numerous molecules that promote cancer growth, including those for which no drugs exist, at the same time to achieve better therapies," said Abounader, a professor at UVA's School of Medicine in the Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Cancer Biology, as well as its Comprehensive Cancer Center and Center for RNA Science and Medicine. "We are hoping to translate our findings into future clinical trials for patients with glioblastoma and other brain tumors."

Why Glioblastoma Is So Difficult to Treat

Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. It claims more than 13,000 lives in the United States each year. One reason it is so difficult to treat is that cancer cells spread into surrounding healthy brain tissue, making it nearly impossible for surgeons to remove the entire tumor.

Another major challenge is the brain's natural "blood-brain barrier." This protective system helps shield the brain from harmful substances, including toxins and infectious agents. Unfortunately, it also blocks many drugs that could otherwise be used to attack brain cancer.

Current treatment generally begins with surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Patients then receive radiation therapy and chemotherapy to help control the remaining cancer and extend survival. Despite these efforts, glioblastoma remains exceptionally difficult to manage.

The UVA researchers are pursuing a different strategy. Instead of relying on drugs that target individual cancer-related processes, their approach uses microRNAs, small pieces of genetic material capable of suppressing the activity of multiple problematic genes at the same time.

By disrupting several genes that help glioblastoma grow and survive, the treatment could potentially slow or even stop tumor growth. This ability to target multiple cancer-driving mechanisms is especially important because combining several conventional cancer drugs can produce harmful side effects. In addition, many of the molecules involved in cancer growth cannot currently be targeted by available medications.

Using Ultrasound to Deliver Cancer-Fighting Molecules

Getting these genetic molecules into the brain presents another major challenge. To overcome it, Abounader's team uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), allowing researchers to direct sound waves precisely toward the intended area.

The ultrasound works with tiny "microbubbles" to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier. This creates a brief opportunity for nanoparticles carrying the microRNAs to pass through the barrier and enter the brain, where they can act on genes involved in tumor growth.

The researchers tested this approach in laboratory experiments and animal models of glioblastoma. Their findings showed that the microRNA treatment slowed tumor growth and helped the animals survive longer.

Although these results are encouraging, the strategy remains experimental and will require additional research before it can be evaluated in human patients. Abounader believes the findings provide an important early indication that the technology could eventually benefit people with glioblastoma and potentially those with other types of cancer.

"This approach could have broad applications for several brain and other human diseases," Abounader said. "We and many others are intensively working to lighten the burden of cancer, and hopefully also completely cure it, but this requires a continued investment in cancer and medical research."

UVA Expands Focused Ultrasound Cancer Research

UVA Health has been at the forefront of focused ultrasound research since the technology's early development. Over the years, its scientists have built an extensive research program investigating how precisely directed sound waves might be used to treat a wide range of medical conditions.

Recognizing the technology's potential in cancer care, UVA partnered with the Charlottesville-based Focused Ultrasound Foundation to establish the Focused Ultrasound Immuno-Oncology (FUSION) Center. It is the first center in the world devoted specifically to investigating how focused ultrasound can be combined with cancer immunotherapy. Researchers believe this combination could lead to major advances in cancer treatment during the 21st century.

The effort also supports the broader missions of UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center and UVA's Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology, both of which are working to improve care through new medical discoveries.

UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center is among just 57 cancer centers nationwide to receive the National Cancer Institute's prestigious "comprehensive" designation. The recognition reflects its excellence in cancer research and patient care.

The Manning Institute was established to speed the discovery and development of new medicines and potential cures for some of the most difficult diseases. Its work is supported by a statewide clinical trials network designed to make emerging treatments more accessible to patients as they move through research and testing.

Study Findings and Research Support

Abounader and his colleagues published their experimental approach and initial laboratory findings in JCI, the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The study is open access and can be read free of charge.

The research team included Shekhar Saha, Ying Zhang, Myron K. Gibert Jr., Collin Dube, Farina Hanif, Elizabeth Qian Xu Mulcahy, Sylwia Bednarek, Yunan Sun, Pawel Marcinkiewicz, Xiantao Wang, Gijung Kwak, Ahsan H. Polash, Haolin Li, Kadie Hudson, Manikarna Dinda, Tapas Saha, Matthew McCord, Fadila Guessous, Nichola Cruickshanks, Rossymar Rivera Colon, Lily Dell'Olio, Rajitha Anbu, Wenjie Liu, Songy Choi, Benjamin Kefas, Pankaj Kumar, Alexander L. Klibanov, David Schiff, Jung Soo Suk, Justin Hanes, Jamie Mata, Markus Hafner and Abounader. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Cancer Institute through grants U01 CA220841 and P30 CA044579, along with the NIH's National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke through grants R01 NS122222 and R21 NS122136. Additional support was provided by a UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center pilot grant, a Schiff Foundation grant, the Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation, and the Focused Ultrasound Foundation.

This approach addresses major treatment challenges like the blood-brain barrier and targets multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously, potentially improving outcomes for many patients. The research is detailed, with promising lab and animal results, and aims for future clinical trials, indicating broad and meaningful impact on public health.

They use focused ultrasound (a type of sound wave), tiny particles called nanoparticles, and special genetic molecules called microRNAs. The ultrasound opens the brain’s protective barrier just long enough to let the nanoparticles deliver microRNAs into the brain. These microRNAs can block several cancer-causing genes at once.

articles.title: Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch
articles.summary: A massive study of nearly 486,000 adults found that regularly drinking tea was associated with an 11% lower risk of heart and blood vessel diseases. The lowest risk was linked to drinking roughly six to eight cups per day, with black tea showing more consistent benefits than green tea.
articles.content:
Drinking tea regularly may offer important benefits for your heart and blood vessels, according to a massive study involving nearly 500,000 adults. Researchers found that people who consumed tea regularly had a lower risk of developing several vascular diseases compared with those who did not drink tea.

However, the findings also revealed some unexpected differences. The type of tea, how strong it was, and even the temperature at which it was consumed were all associated with vascular health. While certain tea drinking habits were linked to a lower risk of disease, drinking tea at extremely high temperatures appeared to have the opposite association.

The research, published in the Journal of Internal Medicine, provides new insights into how an everyday beverage may be connected to long-term cardiovascular health.

Nearly 500,000 Adults Reveal a Link Between Tea and Vascular Health

The study included 485,934 adults in China who were followed for a median of 9.05 years. During that period, researchers recorded 14,863 cases involving several types of vascular disease.

These conditions included cardiovascular disease, which affects the heart and blood vessels, and cerebrovascular disease, which involves blood vessels that supply the brain. The researchers also examined pulmonary heart disease, a condition in which problems involving the lungs or their blood vessels place strain on the heart, and peripheral artery disease, which occurs when arteries carrying blood to areas such as the legs become narrowed or blocked.

Although these conditions affect different parts of the body, they share an important feature: they interfere with the circulation of blood, which delivers oxygen and nutrients to organs and tissues.

When the researchers compared tea drinking habits with the incidence of these diseases, they found that regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of the combined vascular outcomes.

The relationship also appeared to vary with the amount consumed. Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk occurred at approximately six to eight cups per day.

This does not necessarily mean that drinking more tea directly prevents disease or that everyone should consume that amount. Because the research was observational, it could identify connections between tea drinking and health outcomes but could not establish that tea itself was responsible for the differences.

Black Tea vs. Green Tea: Does the Type Matter?

One particularly interesting finding involved the type of tea participants consumed.

Black tea showed more consistent associations with a reduced risk of vascular disease than green tea. This suggests that different varieties of tea may not have identical relationships with cardiovascular health.

Both black and green tea come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, but they undergo different processing methods. Black tea is typically allowed to undergo extensive oxidation, a chemical process that changes the composition of compounds in the leaves, while green tea is processed to limit oxidation.

Tea naturally contains plant compounds known as polyphenols, which have attracted scientific interest because of their antioxidant properties and potential effects on blood vessel function. Antioxidants can help limit certain types of cellular damage caused by reactive molecules.

However, the study does not establish whether these compounds explain the observed differences between black and green tea.

Tea strength also appeared to matter. Participants who drank tea of moderate strength had the lowest associated vascular disease risk, suggesting that stronger tea was not necessarily linked to greater benefits.

Drinking Tea Too Hot May Carry Unexpected Risks

Perhaps the most surprising finding concerned tea temperature.

Although regular tea consumption was generally associated with a reduced risk of vascular disease, drinking tea described as "burning hot" was linked to an increased risk.

The result suggests that the temperature of tea may be an important consideration alongside how much people drink and which variety they prefer.

Very hot beverages can expose tissues in the mouth and digestive tract to high temperatures, but the study did not establish the biological mechanism behind the observed vascular risk. It also did not identify a specific temperature at which tea becomes harmful.

The findings therefore should not be interpreted as proof that drinking extremely hot tea directly causes vascular disease. They do, however, raise questions about whether certain drinking habits could offset some of the favorable associations seen with regular tea consumption.

Tea, Exercise, and Smoking Habits May Work Together

The researchers also examined how tea consumption related to other lifestyle factors, including smoking and physical activity.

Their analysis showed that people who regularly drank tea, were not current smokers, and maintained high levels of physical activity had the lowest vascular disease risk.

"Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk," the authors wrote.

These results highlight the importance of considering overall lifestyle rather than looking at a single food or beverage in isolation.

Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health in several ways, including improving circulation, helping regulate blood pressure, and supporting the function of the heart and blood vessels. Avoiding smoking also reduces exposure to substances that can damage blood vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.

Taken together, the findings suggest that tea drinking may be one component of a broader pattern of habits associated with better vascular health.

Although more research is needed to determine whether tea consumption directly influences disease risk, the study offers encouraging evidence that this widely consumed beverage is associated with cardiovascular health. It also highlights an important distinction: when it comes to tea, the amount, variety, strength, and temperature may all be worth considering.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a large-scale, long-term study involving nearly 500,000 adults that found regular tea consumption is associated with an 11% lower risk of vascular diseases, indicating a positive real-world impact on cardiovascular health. The study provides detailed insights on tea type, amount, strength, and temperature, offering meaningful guidance for public health. The scope and significance are broad, affecting general populations given the prevalence of tea drinking and cardiovascular disease.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les maladies du cœur et des vaisseaux sanguins sont fréquentes dans le monde. Beaucoup de gens boivent du thé chaque jour, et les scientifiques ont voulu savoir si le thé pouvait influencer le risque de ces maladies.

Par exemple, le thé noir et le thé de force modérée étaient plus bénéfiques, tandis que le thé très chaud pourrait être nocif. articles.personality_title_es: Gran estudio vincula el consumo regular de té con menor riesgo de enfermedades cardíacas y vasculares
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las enfermedades del corazón y los vasos sanguíneos son problemas comunes en todo el mundo. Muchas personas beben té todos los días, y los científicos querían saber si el té podría afectar el riesgo de estas enfermedades.

**Qué pasó** – Un estudio siguió a casi 486,000 adultos en China durante unos nueve años. Los investigadores observaron con qué frecuencia y qué tipo de té bebían las personas. Encontraron que quienes bebían té regularmente tenían un 11% menos de riesgo de desarrollar enfermedades del corazón y vasos sanguíneos en comparación con quienes no bebían té. El riesgo más bajo se observó en personas que bebían aproximadamente de seis a ocho tazas al día. El té negro mostró beneficios más constantes que el té verde. Sin embargo, beber té a temperaturas muy altas se relacionó con un mayor riesgo de estas enfermedades.

**Impacto** – Este estudio es uno de los más grandes que conecta el consumo de té con la salud cardiovascular. Muestra que no solo importa beber té, sino también la cantidad, el tipo y hasta la temperatura. Por ejemplo, el té negro y el té de fuerza moderada fueron más beneficiosos, mientras que el té muy caliente podría ser dañino. Los resultados también sugieren que beber té junto con no fumar y mantenerse activo puede reducir aún más el riesgo.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren saber por qué el té muy caliente podría aumentar el riesgo y si los compuestos especiales del té negro ayudan a proteger los vasos sanguíneos. Más estudios podrían explicar cómo el té afecta el cuerpo y guiar hábitos más saludables para beber té.

**Frase resumen** – Beber regularmente de seis a ocho tazas de té negro o té de fuerza moderada, sin tomarlo demasiado caliente, está relacionado con un menor riesgo de enfermedades cardíacas y vasculares, especialmente cuando se combina con hábitos de vida saludables.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day
articles.summary: A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.
articles.content:
Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake."

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance."

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a well-conducted scientific study demonstrating that daily consumption of peanuts improves brain insulin responsiveness and memory-related brain functions in older adults, which has broad implications for aging populations and cognitive health. The study uses rigorous methods and provides detailed findings, indicating a meaningful, tangible benefit for public health.
articles.personality_title: Eating peanuts daily may boost memory and brain health in older adults
articles.personality_presentation:

**What happened** – Scientists at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands studied 31 adults aged 60 to 75. For 16 weeks, participants ate about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts every day. Using brain scans and memory tests, researchers found that peanut eating improved how certain brain areas responded to insulin, especially in parts important for memory.

**Impact** – This is important because better insulin response in these brain regions may help protect memory and thinking skills as people age. The study also builds on earlier research showing that peanuts increase blood flow in the brain and improve verbal memory. The findings suggest peanuts offer multiple nutrients that support brain health, including fats, fiber, vitamins, and a special amino acid called L-arginine.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope future studies will explore how peanuts affect brain health over longer times and in larger groups. They also want to learn which peanut nutrients are most helpful and how peanut eating might fit into everyday diets to support aging brains.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Eating two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for several weeks can improve memory-related brain functions by enhancing insulin response in older adults.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En vieillissant, le cerveau devient souvent moins sensible à l’insuline, une hormone qui aide les cellules nerveuses à grandir et à communiquer. Cette baisse de sensibilité peut affecter la mémoire et être liée à des maladies comme Alzheimer.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs du Centre médical universitaire de Maastricht aux Pays-Bas ont étudié 31 adultes âgés de 60 à 75 ans. Pendant 16 semaines, les participants ont mangé environ deux portions de cacahuètes grillées sans sel chaque jour. Grâce à des scanners cérébraux et des tests de mémoire, ils ont constaté une meilleure réponse à l’insuline dans des zones du cerveau importantes pour la mémoire.

**Impact** – Cela est important car une meilleure réponse à l’insuline dans ces régions peut aider à protéger la mémoire et les capacités intellectuelles avec l’âge. Cette étude complète des recherches antérieures montrant que les cacahuètes augmentent le flux sanguin cérébral et améliorent la mémoire verbale. Les résultats suggèrent que plusieurs nutriments des cacahuètes, comme des graisses, des fibres, des vitamines et un acide aminé appelé L-arginine, soutiennent la santé du cerveau.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs souhaitent approfondir les effets des cacahuètes sur le cerveau sur de plus longues périodes et avec plus de participants. Ils veulent aussi identifier quels nutriments sont les plus bénéfiques et comment intégrer les cacahuètes dans l’alimentation quotidienne pour aider le cerveau des personnes âgées.

**Phrase clé** – Manger deux portions quotidiennes de cacahuètes grillées sans sel pendant plusieurs semaines peut améliorer la fonction cérébrale liée à la mémoire en renforçant la réponse à l’insuline chez les personnes âgées.
articles.personality_title_es: Comer cacahuates a diario puede mejorar la memoria y la salud cerebral en adultos mayores
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – A medida que las personas envejecen, su cerebro suele responder menos a la insulina, una hormona que ayuda a las células nerviosas a crecer y comunicarse. Esta menor respuesta puede afectar la memoria y está relacionada con enfermedades como el Alzheimer.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos del Centro Médico Universitario de Maastricht en los Países Bajos estudiaron a 31 adultos de entre 60 y 75 años. Durante 16 semanas, los participantes comieron aproximadamente dos porciones diarias de cacahuates tostados sin sal. Usando escáneres cerebrales y pruebas de memoria, los investigadores encontraron que comer cacahuates mejoró la respuesta a la insulina en partes del cerebro importantes para la memoria.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque una mejor respuesta a la insulina en estas áreas puede ayudar a proteger la memoria y las habilidades mentales con la edad. El estudio se basa en investigaciones anteriores que mostraron que los cacahuates aumentan el flujo sanguíneo cerebral y mejoran la memoria verbal. Los resultados sugieren que varios nutrientes en los cacahuates, como grasas, fibra, vitaminas y un aminoácido llamado L-arginina, apoyan la salud del cerebro.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren estudiar cómo los cacahuates afectan la salud cerebral durante más tiempo y en grupos más grandes. También buscan identificar qué nutrientes son más beneficiosos y cómo incluir cacahuates en la dieta diaria para apoyar el cerebro en la vejez.

**Frase clave** – Comer dos porciones diarias de cacahuates tostados sin sal durante varias semanas puede mejorar las funciones cerebrales relacionadas con la memoria al aumentar la respuesta a la insulina en adultos mayores.

articles.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
articles.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.
articles.content:
An ancient ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging a long-standing theory about where the ancestors of modern apes, including humans, first evolved. The remarkable find suggests that a crucial chapter of our evolutionary history may have unfolded much farther north than scientists previously believed.

The newly identified species, named Masripithecus moghraensis, lived approximately 17 to 18 million years ago during the Early Miocene. Its fossilized remains were recovered from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt, making it the first definitive fossil ape ever discovered in North Africa.

The discovery, described in a study published March 26, 2026, in Science, comes from an international team at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (Egypt) and the University of Southern California (USA). Their findings suggest that northern Africa and the Middle East may have played a central role in the emergence of the evolutionary lineage that eventually gave rise to all living apes.

A Missing Piece of the Ape Evolutionary Puzzle

For decades, scientists believed that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated primarily in regions farther south in Africa. Fossil sites in North Africa had produced remains of ancient monkeys from the Early Miocene, but researchers had never found definitive evidence of apes from the same period.

That gap helped shape prevailing theories about ape evolution. Although younger ape fossils have been discovered across Africa, Europe, and Asia, their evolutionary relationships and geographic origins remain subjects of scientific debate.

The newly discovered Egyptian fossil may help explain what was missing from this picture.

"We spent five years searching for this kind of fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that something is missing -- and North Africa holds that missing piece," said Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University and senior author of the study.

The discovery is especially important for understanding the origins of crown Hominoidea, the evolutionary group that includes the last common ancestor of all living apes and its descendants. Today, that group encompasses gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

Scientists suspect that the incomplete geographic distribution of ancient fossils has obscured important details about when and where this group first emerged.

An 18-Million-Year-Old Ape With Unusual Teeth

The fossils were uncovered during expeditions in 2023 and 2024 by researchers from the Sallam Lab at Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt.

The team named the species Masripithecus moghraensis. Its genus name combines Masr (مصر), the Arabic name for Egypt, with píthēkos, the Greek word for ape. The species name honors Wadi Moghra, where the fossils were found.

Although the remains consist only of lower jaw material, they contain an unusual combination of anatomical features that distinguishes the animal from other apes of similar age.

The jaw is exceptionally sturdy, with remarkably large canine and premolar teeth. Its molars also have rounded chewing surfaces covered in pronounced textures. These characteristics offer valuable clues about the foods the animal could eat and how it survived in its environment.

Researchers believe Masripithecus primarily consumed fruit but had teeth powerful enough to process tougher foods when necessary. This dietary flexibility may have been an important survival advantage.

"Together, they suggest that Masripithecus was adapted for versatility. The study interprets its chewing anatomy as evidence of a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet, with the ability to process harder foods such as nuts or seeds when needed. This flexibility would have helped Masripithecus to thrive at a time when climatic changes were leading to more pronounced seasonality in northern Africa and Arabia," said Shorouq Al-Ashqar, a researcher at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center and a first author of the study.

As seasonal differences became more pronounced, the availability of certain foods likely changed throughout the year. An ape capable of eating a wider range of foods would have been better equipped to cope with those fluctuations.

A Discovery That Challenges the Ape Family Tree

The importance of Masripithecus extends well beyond its unusual anatomy. When researchers examined where the species belonged on the evolutionary family tree, they uncovered a surprising result.

Their analysis suggests that Masripithecus was more closely related to living apes than any known ape species from the Early Miocene of East Africa.

To investigate these relationships, the team used advanced statistical techniques known as Bayesian methods. These approaches allow scientists to compare different evolutionary possibilities and estimate how strongly the available evidence supports each one.

The researchers combined anatomical information from living and extinct apes with genetic evidence from living species. They also incorporated the geological ages of fossil specimens, helping them estimate when different evolutionary branches separated.

By bringing these sources of evidence together, the scientists reconstructed relationships among ancient and modern apes and explored where their shared ancestors may have lived.

The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the evolutionary roots of all living apes were centered in or around East Africa.

Could North Africa Be the Birthplace of Modern Apes?

Additional analyses of ancient animal distributions pointed toward northern Africa and the Middle East as the most likely geographic home of the common ancestor of all living apes.

That ancestor is estimated to have lived during the Early Miocene, an interval spanning roughly 23 million to 16 million years ago. This was an important period in primate evolution, when early ape lineages were diversifying, and environments were undergoing substantial changes.

Geography may help explain why this region was so important.

Millions of years ago, Africa, Arabia, and Asia were moving toward a new geological arrangement. As the African and Arabian tectonic plates traveled northward and approached the final stages of their collision with Asia, the connections between these landmasses began to change.

Sea levels also rose and fell, periodically reducing the stretches of water that separated different regions. At certain times, these changes made it easier for animals to move between Africa and Eurasia.

Northern Africa and the Middle East therefore occupied a potentially crucial position in the movement and evolution of ancient mammals, including apes.

The discovery of Masripithecus helps connect previously separated fossil records from Africa and Eurasia. Its presence suggests that apes were already evolving into distinct forms in this region before new land connections made it possible for them to expand into Europe and Asia.

Rather than being a peripheral location in ape evolution, the region may have been an important center of evolutionary diversification.

Scientists Rethink Where Our Ancient Ape Ancestors Lived

The findings have even prompted some of the researchers to reconsider ideas they held throughout their careers.

Erik Seiffert, a paleontologist at the University of Southern California and co-author of the study, explained how the evidence has changed his understanding of ape origins.

"For my entire career, I considered it probable that the common ancestor of all living apes lived in or around East Africa. But this new discovery, and our new and novel analyses of hominoid phylogeny and biogeography, now strongly challenge that idea. And, importantly, the likelihood of this scenario doesn't depend on Masripithecus -- but it is very much consistent with it."

Importantly, the researchers are not claiming that Masripithecus was a direct ancestor of humans or even necessarily the direct ancestor of living apes. Instead, its position on the evolutionary family tree provides evidence about where the broader ancestral lineage may have originated.

The distinction matters because humans emerged much later in evolutionary history. The Egyptian fossil offers clues to an earlier stage, when the distant ancestors shared by humans and other living apes were evolving.

The team's findings also suggest that the traditional emphasis on East African fossils may have provided an incomplete view of this much older evolutionary story.

More Evolutionary Secrets May Be Hidden in Egypt

Although the discovery offers compelling new evidence, scientists still have much to learn about Masripithecus and the early history of modern apes.

Only part of the animal's jaw has been recovered, leaving important questions about its overall appearance, body size, movement, and behavior unanswered. Additional fossils could provide a more complete picture of how this ancient species lived and how it relates to other early apes.

The researchers believe that further exploration of North Africa and the Middle East could reveal additional species and help clarify when and where the major branches of the modern ape family tree began to emerge.

For now, Masripithecus moghraensis offers a striking reminder that even fundamental ideas about our distant evolutionary past can change when scientists uncover evidence in places that have received relatively little attention.

A fossil jaw preserved for nearly 18 million years may be helping scientists piece together a chapter of evolutionary history that was missing all along.

articles.personality_title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt challenges ideas about ape origins
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long believed that the earliest ancestors of modern apes, including humans, evolved mainly in East Africa. Fossils of ancient monkeys were found in North Africa, but no clear ape fossils from that time had been discovered there until now.

**What happened** – Researchers found a 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil in northern Egypt called Masripithecus moghraensis. This fossil, made up of a lower jaw with unusual teeth, was uncovered in 2023 and 2024 at Wadi Moghra. It is the first definite ape fossil from North Africa dating to the Early Miocene period.

**Impact** – This discovery suggests that modern apes may have first evolved in North Africa or the Middle East, not East Africa as previously thought. The fossil’s features show it was a flexible eater, able to survive changing climates. Using new analysis methods, scientists found that Masripithecus is closer to living apes than similar fossils from East Africa, changing the story of ape evolution.

**What's next step** – Researchers plan to search for more fossils in North Africa and the Middle East to better understand how early apes lived and evolved. Finding more evidence could reshape how scientists view the spread and development of ape ancestors before humans appeared.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The discovery of Masripithecus moghraensis in Egypt offers new clues that the birthplace of modern apes may lie in North Africa and the Middle East, not East Africa as once believed.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un fossile de singe ancien en Égypte remet en question l'origine des singes modernes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques pensaient que les premiers ancêtres des singes modernes, y compris les humains, avaient évolué principalement en Afrique de l'Est. Des fossiles de singes anciens avaient été trouvés en Afrique du Nord, mais aucun fossile clair de singe de cette époque n’avait été découvert jusqu’à présent.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs ont découvert un fossile de singe vieux de 17 à 18 millions d’années dans le nord de l’Égypte, nommé Masripithecus moghraensis. Ce fossile, constitué d’une mâchoire inférieure avec des dents particulières, a été trouvé en 2023 et 2024 à Wadi Moghra. C’est le premier fossile de singe datant du Miocène précoce en Afrique du Nord.

**Impact** – Cette découverte suggère que les singes modernes ont peut-être évolué en Afrique du Nord ou au Moyen-Orient, et non en Afrique de l’Est comme on le croyait. Les caractéristiques du fossile montrent qu’il pouvait manger différents types d’aliments, ce qui l’aidait à survivre aux changements climatiques. Des analyses avancées indiquent que Masripithecus est plus proche des singes vivants que ceux trouvés en Afrique de l’Est, changeant ainsi notre compréhension de l’évolution des singes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs souhaitent trouver d’autres fossiles en Afrique du Nord et au Moyen-Orient pour mieux comprendre la vie et l’évolution des premiers singes. Ces nouvelles découvertes pourraient modifier notre vision sur la répartition et le développement des ancêtres des singes avant l’apparition des humains.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La découverte de Masripithecus moghraensis en Égypte apporte des indices nouveaux que le berceau des singes modernes pourrait être en Afrique du Nord et au Moyen-Orient, et non en Afrique de l’Est comme on le pensait.
articles.personality_title_es: Fósil antiguo de simio en Egipto desafía ideas sobre el origen de los simios modernos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos creyeron que los ancestros más antiguos de los simios modernos, incluidos los humanos, evolucionaron principalmente en África Oriental. Se habían encontrado fósiles de monos antiguos en el norte de África, pero nunca fósiles claros de simios de esa época.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores descubrieron un fósil de simio de 17 a 18 millones de años en el norte de Egipto llamado Masripithecus moghraensis. Este fósil, formado por una mandíbula inferior con dientes especiales, fue hallado en 2023 y 2024 en Wadi Moghra. Es el primer fósil definitivo de simio del Mioceno temprano en África del Norte.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo sugiere que los simios modernos podrían haberse originado en África del Norte o el Medio Oriente, no en África Oriental como se pensaba. Las características del fósil indican que este simio podía comer diferentes tipos de alimentos, lo que le ayudaba a sobrevivir en climas cambiantes. Con métodos avanzados, los científicos encontraron que Masripithecus está más relacionado con los simios vivos que otros fósiles similares de África Oriental, cambiando la historia de la evolución de los simios.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean buscar más fósiles en África del Norte y el Medio Oriente para entender mejor cómo vivían y evolucionaban los primeros simios. Más descubrimientos podrían cambiar la visión científica sobre la expansión y desarrollo de los ancestros de los simios antes de la aparición humana.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El descubrimiento de Masripithecus moghraensis en Egipto ofrece nuevas pistas de que el origen de los simios modernos podría estar en África del Norte y el Medio Oriente, no en África Oriental como se creía.
